name: RapidWeaver Elements
subcategory: desktop visual site builder for Mac
tagline: A Mac desktop app for building and publishing static websites from visual components, no hosting account required.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Elements is not a SaaS, it is a local app that spits out static files and pushes them over FTP or SFTP, so there is no network or data moat protecting it. What it sells is the editing experience: a visual canvas, a component system, theme styling, live preview, and a publish button that does not make you think about build tooling. An agent can absolutely give you the output side in a weekend: an Astro project, a block-based page format, a small browser editor, and a deploy script. What it cannot give you in one session is a decade of component polish, or the part where the canvas never breaks when you nest things wrong. If you are comfortable in a text editor you probably did not need the app at all, which is a different kind of verdict.
coreLoopDIY: A local Astro project where pages are JSON block lists edited in a small browser UI, previewed live, built to static HTML, and pushed to a server over SFTP.
requirements: a server, S3 bucket, or static host with SFTP or API access
basic comfort running a dev server
whatYouLose: A real visual canvas with drag, drop, snapping, and inline text editing that does not fight you
The component and theme library, plus whatever third-party addons you relied on
Responsive breakpoint controls done by clicking instead of by writing CSS
A publish flow that handles diffing, asset uploads, and failures quietly
Mac-native niceties: offline project files, undo across everything, no terminal
moatNotes: Project files and theme-specific markup mean old sites do not port cleanly, which is most of the reason people stay.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the people who buy desktop site builders are mostly not the people who want a dev server running. They want a document they can open on their Mac, click around in, and publish to the same shared host they have used since 2011. Paying once for an app that keeps that loop intact is a rational trade against maintaining your own toolchain forever, and the DIY version only wins if you actually enjoy the toolchain.
notes: The output is trivially replaceable; the editing experience is the product.
prompt:
Build a local static site builder in an empty folder. Stack: Astro 4 with TypeScript, plus a tiny Express editor server. No database, no accounts, no cloud services, no telemetry.

Structure:
- /src/content/pages/*.json : each page is { slug, title, description, blocks: [] }
- /src/blocks/ : Astro components, one per block type
- /editor/ : the Express app and its browser UI

Block types to implement, exactly these: hero (heading, subheading, image, optional button), richText (markdown string), imageText (image left or right, markdown body), gallery (list of images, CSS grid), cards (list of title, body, optional link), cta (heading, button), spacer (height in rem), rawHtml (escape hatch).

Rendering: one dynamic Astro route builds every page from its JSON, mapping block type to component. Global site config in /site.config.json for site title, nav links, footer text, and three CSS variables for accent, text, and background. Ship one clean responsive stylesheet, system font stack, max width 72ch for text blocks, mobile first, no CSS framework.

Editor: run `npm run editor` to serve a browser UI at localhost:4321 that lists pages, creates and deletes pages, and edits a page as a vertical list of blocks. Per block: a form for its fields, move up, move down, duplicate, delete, and an add-block picker. Save writes the JSON file to disk. Show the Astro dev preview in an iframe beside the form and reload it after save. This is a form-based editor, not a drag-and-drop canvas. Do not fake a canvas.

Images: `/public/uploads`, uploaded via the editor, served as plain files. Generate width and height attributes on insert so layout does not jump.

Publish: `npm run deploy` runs `astro build` then uploads `dist/` over SFTP using ssh2-sftp-client. Read SFTP_HOST, SFTP_USER, SFTP_KEY_PATH, SFTP_REMOTE_PATH from .env. Compare local file hashes against a `.deploystate.json` manifest and upload only changed files. Print what was uploaded and what was skipped. Commit .env.example, never .env.

Also generate: sitemap.xml, robots.txt, per-page meta and Open Graph tags from title and description.

Out of scope, do not build: drag-and-drop canvas, visual breakpoint controls, theme marketplace, plugin API, multi-user editing, blog comments, analytics.

Finish with a README covering install, editor, deploy, and how to add a new block type in under twenty lines of code.
